candidateRows: Human decency precedes religion, while religious doctrine, dogma, and revelation appropriate those human goods and introduce harmful additions.
This metaphor establishes the affirmative theory of the motion and connects religion's claimed goods to its doctrinal harms.
Woodford portrays compassion and hope as a human well that religion contaminates, falsely claims, and uses to support exclusion, subordination, and original sin.
Religion poisons everything when it cannot provide a uniquely good contribution without also introducing something bad.
The passage supplies the affirmative's operative definition and its principal test for every claimed religious benefit.
Woodford disclaims the claim that religion never does good, then requires a proposed benefit to be good, uniquely religious, and free of harmful conditions.
Christianity distinguishes self-exalting religion from a divine movement of outward blessing and embeds criticism of corrupt religious power.
This distinction directly contests the affirmative's treatment of religion as a single contaminating category and frames the negative case.
Woodford's claim that religious doctrine necessarily contaminates preexisting human goods.
Scrivener contrasts Babel with Abraham, invokes prophets against power, and presents Jesus as a victim of religious violence at Christianity's center.
Christian devotion redirects service toward human beings as divine images and historically generated distinctive institutions of compassion and reform.
The passage offers the negative's principal counterexample to the claim that religion adds no uniquely good and clean contribution.
Woodford's three-hurdle contention that religious goods are neither unique nor free from accompanying poison.
Scrivener says union with Jesus produced a community serving neighbors, opposing infanticide, pederasty, and gladiatorial games, and advancing human flourishing.
The poison behind religious and secular atrocities is a general human problem, while Christianity supplies standards for condemning it and an antidote in Jesus.
This move relocates culpability from religion specifically to humanity generally and gives Christianity a corrective rather than poisonous role.
Woodford's attribution of recurring moral harms specifically to religious doctrine, dogma, and revelation.
Scrivener acknowledges inquisitions, crusades, and abuse, argues Christianity can condemn them, then cites revolutionary and totalitarian violence as secular parallels.
Islamic community and charity illustrate how a religious benefit can be accompanied by doctrinal harms involving women and gay people.
The example operationalizes the affirmative's central test and challenges the negative to classify explicit doctrinal harms as poison.
Scrivener's claim that religious community can generate outward blessing, compassion, and human flourishing.
Woodford grants Ramadan's communal and charitable value but argues that Islamic teachings concerning testimony and homosexuality show the benefit does not come clean.
Both debaters judge communities by a highest ideal, but Christianity identifies that governing rational ideal with Jesus rather than leaving it ungrounded.
The move shifts the dispute from identifying isolated harms to explaining the authority by which good and bad are judged.
Woodford's request to classify harmful Islamic teachings as poison while crediting secularly available community goods.
Scrivener says both sides share judgments shaped by Christian society, but differ over whether rationality itself or Jesus grounds their highest standard.
Conceding that one Islamic practice is poisonous is compatible with the motion because religious community is not unique and introduces doctrinal harm.
This reply prevents the negative's literal reading of everything from displacing the affirmative's stated unique-good-without-harm criterion.
Scrivener's objection that Islam cannot poison everything if it contains acknowledged good communal aspects.
Woodford agrees community can be good but calls it a human and secularly reproducible good, accusing religion of claiming ownership of what it did not create.
Christian political dominance failed to abolish slavery despite having the power to do so, showing that its later abolitionist association does not vindicate it.
The historical argument directly challenges abolition as a uniquely Christian achievement and tests doctrine against sustained institutional conduct.
Scrivener's contention that the abolitionist movement was a remarkably and profoundly religious effort.
Woodford argues Christians possessed governing power for many centuries and enacted some reforms, yet did not categorically prohibit owning human beings.
New Testament slave commands and comparison with Hammurabi undermine the claim that biblical religion improved slavery over surrounding ancient systems.
The move contests the negative's strongest historical counterexample by arguing that scripture endorsed harsh and permanent slavery rather than improving it.
Scrivener's claim that biblical law ameliorated ancient slavery and that the New Testament supplied a liberating trajectory.
Woodford cites obedience commands for slaves, contrasts biblical rules with a shorter Hammurabi debt-slavery term, and attributes later advances to the Enlightenment.
Biblical slavery law was worse than the earlier Code of Hammurabi in material respects, undermining the claim that Christianity improved slavery.
This historical comparison directly contests the claim that Christianity improved inherited institutions and supplies a concrete example of religious doctrine worsening them.
Glen's claim that biblical and Christian developments improved ancient slavery practices.
After citing New Testament commands for slaves to obey harsh masters, Stephen compares biblical rules with Hammurabi's earlier limits and protections.
Human brutality, pride, violence, and domination precede religion, while Christianity supplies a decisive basis for rejecting that inherited condition.
The move directly reverses the motion's causal account by locating poison within humanity and presenting Christianity as the source of moral transformation.
Stephen's claim that religion adds poison to otherwise available human decency and worsens institutions such as slavery.
Glen answers the slavery comparison by invoking original sin, describing a universally brutal pre-Christian world, and asking what secular turning point grounds reform.
Christian monogamous marriage constrained elite male sexual power and thereby elevated and protected women and children.
It offers a specific institutional mechanism by which Christian teaching allegedly produced social benefits, directly supporting the Christian-humanist side of the motion.
Stephen's comparison alleging that earlier non-Christian law gave women stronger divorce and property rights.
In response to questions about women's rights, Glen argues that Christian marital permanence and monogamy restrained male exploitation for families' benefit.
Christian scripture harmed women, and Glen's humane motif requires moving away from explicit biblical doctrines rather than deriving decency from them.
The move closely states the affirmative theory: harmful doctrine and revelation corrupt decency, while humane Christianity succeeds only by importing values into scripture.
Glen's argument that Christian sexual ethics and monogamous marriage raised the status of women and children.
Stephen concedes that religions can do good, then cites restrictions on women and argues that Glen must detach his compassionate presentation from biblical text.
Slavery is wrong because enslaving a person made in God's image violates humanity's divinely granted status and vocation.
It supplies the requested Christian moral foundation for abolition and connects sacred anthropology directly to the debate's recurring test case of slavery.
Stephen's challenge that Glen had not adequately explained or doctrinally grounded why slavery is morally wrong.
During the dispute over whether moral grounding is relevant, Glen gives the image of God and human dominion as abolitionist doctrines.
Christian Trinitarian theology escapes the Euthyphro dilemma because goodness is the eternal loving life of God rather than an arbitrary command.
This is the con side's developed answer to the debate's metaethical challenge and supports the claim that Christianity grounds love and moral judgment non-arbitrarily.
Stephen's Euthyphro challenge that divine morality is either arbitrary or dependent upon goodness external to God.
After both speakers formulate the dilemma, Glen identifies God with goodness and love, then explains evil as violation of the loving reality shaping creation.
Centuries of Christian institutional dominance did not abolish slavery, despite Christians possessing the power to make major social changes.
The argument tests Christian humanitarian causation against institutional history and challenges the contention that Christian dominion uniquely liberated enslaved people.
Glen's claim that Christian doctrine supplied the decisive moral basis and historical impetus for ending slavery.
Following the metaethical exchange, Stephen returns to historical outcomes and asks why fifth- and sixth-century Christian power did not emancipate slaves.
Paul's advice to slaves worked within an existing slave society while Christian equality and gradual transformation ultimately ended the slave trade.
This provides the con side's direct interpretation of an apparently pro-slavery text and its causal account of how Christianity transforms oppressive structures.
Stephen's use of Ephesians commanding slave obedience as evidence that Christianity endorsed and perpetuated slavery.
Glen argues that church members were equal under Christ, ordinary conduct continued outside church, and yeast-like reform worked gradually through society.
Christian gradualism cannot excuse slavery because God and Christian rulers made radical institutional changes elsewhere while leaving slavery intact until the Enlightenment era.
The argument attacks a central Christian defense of harmful doctrine by showing alleged selective reform and linking eventual opposition to declining Christian authority.
Glen's claim that Christianity appropriately transformed slave society gradually through an internally egalitarian, yeast-like movement.
Stephen argues that Jesus could challenge establishments and Christians rapidly changed other institutions, making their prolonged toleration of slavery especially damaging.
Christianity uniquely scaled compassion beyond kin and tribe by teaching love of enemies and concern for the weak despite evolutionary pressures against such pity.
This directly supports the claim that Christianity generated the universal compassion central to modern humane ideals rather than merely borrowing ordinary human decency.
Stephen's suggestion that human beings cared for one another before Christianity and that humane conduct does not require Jesus.
Glen distinguishes natural care for relatives and groups from concern for outsiders, arguing that Christianity made enemy-love and pity culturally admirable at scale.
Divine commands involving the conquest of Canaan expose the failure of grounding morality solely in God's nature.
The argument contests Christianity's proposed moral foundation by testing whether an apparently atrocious divine command becomes good merely through its divine source.
Glen's claim that equality and moral goodness are grounded in God and God's loving nature.
After the grounding dispute crosses the chunk boundary, Stephen introduces a new biblical test case concerning commands against Canaanite men, women, and children.
Christian scripture explicitly permitted hereditary slavery, and Christian institutions retained it for centuries rather than promptly abolishing it.
This move supplies doctrinal and historical support for the motion by arguing that Christianity preserved a serious moral harm instead of correcting it.
Glen's appeal to nonliteral ancient idiom and Christianity's eventual long-term contribution to abolition.
Stephen shifts from Glen's hyperbole defense of conquest to slavery law, then argues that abolition arrived only after many Christian centuries while dissenters faced persecution.
Without an objective moral foundation, shared present agreement cannot explain why slavery or caste hierarchy is genuinely wrong.
The move attacks the pro side's evaluative standard and supports the counterclaim that religious moral ideas made slavery's wrongness universally intelligible.
Stephen's contention that agreement about harms is sufficient without resolving a complete metaethical theory.
Following Stephen's refusal to select a metaethical system, Glen tests agreement-based morality against caste hierarchy and presents abolition as a religious contribution.
Christian doctrine entrenched slavery, while later Christian abolitionists became morally persuasive only by retreating from doctrine toward broad humane themes.
This directly advances the motion's distinction between prior human decency and the doctrines, dogmas, and revelations alleged to corrupt or obstruct it.
Glen's claim that abolitionism was religious throughout and demonstrates that religion does not poison everything.
Stephen answers the abolition argument with a historical account in which authoritative Christian sources reinforced slavery until institutional power weakened and doctrine was softened.
The doctrine that humans bear God's image generated charity, opposition to infanticide and slavery, scientific confidence, and the modern ideal of humane compassion.
The move offers a concrete religious doctrine as a source of central moral and institutional goods, directly denying that doctrine merely poisons preexisting decency.
Stephen's assertion that humane reform required removing Christian doctrine, dogma, and revelation.
In response to the demand for doctrinal receipts, Glen presents the image of God as foundational to compassion, equal human worth, reform, and intelligible inquiry into nature.
Christianity's claimed necessity for social goods is testable by identifying moral goods supplied by non-Christian people and cultures.
The move challenges the necessity claim underlying the con case and argues that compassion can exist independently before religion modifies or poisons it.
Glen's claim that sacred Christian ideals uniquely ground modern compassion and restrain coercive moral transgression.
Stephen asks for a morally good feature wholly independent of Christianity; Glen cites lessons from non-Christian cultures, which Stephen treats as evidence of prior compassion.
The conquest narratives use military hyperbole, concern judgment against violent cultures and combatants, and culminate in Christianity's prohibition on religious violence.
This is the con side's fullest response to the principal biblical atrocity example used to argue that revelation introduces severe moral poison.
Stephen's portrayal of the Canaan conquest as a divine command to murder children and other noncombatants.
Glen situates the conquest within ancient war rhetoric and a broader narrative of judgment, then argues that Christ removes any Christian warrant for enforcing divine justice violently.
Condemning child sacrifice cannot justify commanding the killing of the same population's children or the taking of its young girls.
The move rebuts the contextual defense by arguing that the stated punishment reproduces the very harm invoked to justify it and adds further exploitation.
Glen's claim that conquest was justified judgment on infanticidal cultures and did not involve killing children.
After Glen's extended account of Canaan, Stephen argues that the narrative's own rationale remains morally incoherent if children are killed for adults' child sacrifice.
Religion pervades rather than poisons humanity because Christian conceptions of persons made equality, abolition, compassion, and moral condemnation historically possible.
The closing states the con side's governing thesis that modern humane ideals cannot be separated from the religious account of humanity that produced them.
Stephen's thesis that ordinary human decency exists prior to religion and is subsequently poisoned by it.
Glen argues that religion cannot be removed from an otherwise intact humanity and grounds judgments against domination and violence in the image and incarnation of God.
Christian moral progress occurs by moving away from specific biblical doctrines toward human compassion, showing that doctrine poisons rather than creates decency.
The closing directly restates the pro mechanism: humane reform emerges as believers distance themselves from revelation while later redescribing reform as Christian.
Glen's closing claim that Christian doctrine and anthropology generated modern compassion, equality, and abolition.
Stephen argues that reformers replace concrete scriptural teaching with increasingly general appeals to Jesus, allowing underlying human love and decency to overcome doctrinal constraints.
